item.title: The VC-Dimension of Visibility in Simple Polygons Is Six
item.description: arXiv:2611.31760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Six targets in a simple polygon can be placed so that, for every subset of the targets, some point in the polygon sees precisely that subset---that is, the polygon shatters the six targets. We prove that no simple polygon shatters seven targets. Together with Valtr's six-target construction, this determines the maximum visibility VC-dimension of a simple polygon to be six (even when the targets must lie in strictly convex position) and improves the previous upper bound of $14$ due to Gilbers and Klein. To rule out a shattered set of seven targets, we classify its convex-hull structure into $74$ cases. In each case, the absence of holes in the polygon forces visibility relations that we encode as Boolean constraints on links and triple orientations. Independently checkable SAT refutations exclude all $74$ cases. The upper-bound proof was derived using AI. A separate Lean 4 formalization independently verifies the upper bound against an axiomatic interface for simple polygons.
item.dc:creator: Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled

item.title: Balanced Voronoi Partitions, Self-Approaching Sequences, and Applications to Efficiently Navigable Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.32667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the following geometric question: given a set $X$ of points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, is it always possible to pick $a,b \in X$ such that their induced Voronoi partition is approximately balanced? I.e., letting $X_a,X_b \subseteq X$ be the sets of points closer to $a$ and $b$ respectively, can we pick $a$ and $b$ such that $\min(|X_a|,|X_b|) \ge \alpha \cdot |X|$ for some $\alpha > 0$? We show that balance $\alpha = \Omega(1/d)$ is always achievable, which is tight up to a constant. The proof is via a reduction to a natural question about self-approaching sequences (SASs): what is the longest sequence of points such that each successive point gets closer to all other points? We show that if there is no balanced Voronoi partition with balance $\alpha$, then one can find an SAS of length $\Omega(1/\alpha)$. We then prove that in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, any SAS has length at most $O(d)$, implying our balanced partitioning result. We discuss extensions beyond Euclidean space: surprisingly, for the $\ell_p$ norm for any constant $p \neq 2$, we show that one cannot achieve balance better than $\mathrm{exp}(-\Omega(d))$. However, a $1/\mathrm{poly}(d)$ bound does hold for point sets with bounded aspect ratio. While we seem to be the first to study the exact problems above, both are closely related to work on navigable search graphs, which admit efficient routing via greedy search, and form the backbone of many modern near neighbor search systems. Results on navigable graphs from the 1990s can be used to give a bound of $\alpha = 1/2^{O(d)}$ for balanced Voronoi partitioning. Our bound exponentially improves this, to $\Omega(1/d)$. Our bound also yields the first construction of navigable graphs under a natural variant of classic greedy routing, with routing time $O(d \log |X|)$. All existing constructions require $\mathrm{exp}(d)$ routing time.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Conroy, Mohammadreza Daneshvaramoli, Cameron Musco, Christopher Musco, Jack Spalding-Jamieson

item.title: Centerpoints with Few Radon Points
item.description: arXiv:2611.32911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A point $z\in\mathbf{R}^d$ is a $\beta$-centerpoint of an $n$-point set $P\subset\mathbf{R}^d$ if every closed halfspace containing $z$ contains at least $\beta n$ points of~$P$. Iterated Radon points yield an $\Omega(1/d^2)$-centerpoint in $\tilde{O}(d^9)$ time: each round replaces a population by Radon points of random $(d+2)$-tuples. Har-Peled and Jones improved the running time to $\tilde{O}(d^7)$. The known analyses certify that \emph{every} point of the population is central. We show that $O(\log^2 d)$ rounds of Radon computations suffice if a \emph{single} Radon point of the last round is output. The analysis tracks, for every $k$, the probability that $k$ random points of a round lie in a common ``bad'' halfspace, so the union bound over halfspaces is taken only once, for the input sample. For points in general position and constant $\varepsilon>0$, a $\frac{1-\varepsilon}{4(d+1)(d+2)}$-centerpoint is computed with constant probability using $O(d^3\log^3 d)$ Radon computations, in $O(d^{3+\omega}\log^3 d)\subseteq O(d^{5.372})$ time ($\omega$: matrix multiplication exponent), or $O(d^6\log^3 d)$ time with Gaussian elimination. The algorithm uses only linear algebra; among strongly polynomial algorithms for centerpoints of quality $1/\mathrm{poly}(d)$ it is the fastest known. For integer input, grid rounding keeps all points polynomially long and still yields an exact centerpoint. Dutta and Pisula obtained quality $\Omega(1/(d\log d\log\log d))$ in weakly polynomial time by solving $\tilde{O}(d^3)$ linear programs, using Tverberg points with $\Theta(\log d)$ parts instead of Radon points. Our analysis extends to rounds of such Tverberg points: for inputs of more than $\tilde{O}(d)$ points, it gives the same quality from $O(d^2\log^4 d\log\log d)$ linear programs in expectation.
item.dc:creator: Guilherme D. da Fonseca, Kunal Dutta

item.title: A Strongly Subquadratic Algorithm for Unique Assembly Verification in the Abstract Tile Assembly Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.32980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show, for the first time, a strongly sub-quadratic algorithm for Unique Assembly Verification (UAV) in the 2D Abstract Tile Assembly Model (aTAM) with any constant temperature. UAV in the 2D aTAM is solvable in $\widetilde{O}(n^{71/36})$. Further, in 3D, we give a logarithmic improvement for UAV to $O(n^2/\sqrt{\log(n+2)})$, and then show that even for assemblies with a constant height of two in 3D (barely 3D), no strongly sub-quadratic algorithm can exist under the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture (OVC) by showing it is coOV-hard. Further, we show that UAV for barely 3D assemblies is P-complete and analyze the result with relation to Circuit-SETH. We show that for UAV, any 3D aTAM system can be simulated by a barely 3D aTAM system. This provides a clear conditional separation between the 2D and 3D problems (even with only two layers), and improves the time complexity for one of the most fundamental problems in algorithmic self-assembly in both 2D and 3D.
item.dc:creator: Tim Wylie

item.title: Hadwiger\'s Covering Conjecture in Three Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.32334v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $K \subset \R^3$ be an arbitrary convex body, that is, a compact convex subset of $\R^3$ with nonempty interior. We prove unconditionally that $K$ can be covered by eight smaller positive homothetic copies of itself: there exist a scalar $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ and translation vectors $v_1, \dots, v_8 \in \R^3$ such that \[ K \subseteq \bigcup_{i=1}^{8} (\lambda K + v_i). \] This resolves Hadwiger's covering conjecture in three dimensions. The proof works in Boltyanski's equivalent boundary illumination formulation and is completely self-contained. Parallelepipeds are covered directly by eight translates of $\frac{2}{3} K$. For any convex body $K$ that is not a parallelepiped, we place its centrally symmetric halved difference body $S = \frac{1}{2}(K - K)$ in John's position ($B^3 \subseteq S$) and show that the spherical average of its support function satisfies $8 \int_{S^2} h_S \, d\sigmatilde < 12$, with equality only for orthogonal cubes. Using outer polyhedral approximations together with Cauchy's planar perimeter formula, the full spherical measure of directions not parallel to any boundary segment of $K$, and lower semicontinuity of curve variation, we find a unit vector $w_* \in S^2$ whose shadow boundary $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ on $K$ itself is a continuous closed curve of $S$-length strictly less than $12$. Splitting $\Shad{K}{w_*}$ into six contiguous arcs of $S$-length strictly less than $2$ and applying Helly's theorem in $\R^3$ illuminates each arc with one direction, while $\pm w_*$ illuminate the remainder of $\partial K$. The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini~4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean~4.
item.dc:creator: Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled, Goran \v{Z}u\v{z}i\'c

item.title: ROVO: Robust Rotation-Only Visual Odometry for UAVs at Low and Moderate Altitudes
item.description: arXiv:2611.32475v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Image noise can confound rotation and translation estimates in monocular visual navigation for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) at low and moderate altitudes, where even small perturbations may cause large errors in translation direction. Inspired by angular cues in long-range visual perception, we propose rotation-only visual odometry (ROVO) for monocular aerial imagery. ROVO estimates pairwise rotations from matched images, robustly averages them over overlapping windows, and aligns consecutive windows through shared frames. By retaining only orientation in the trajectory state, it prevents uncertain landmark depth from propagating to later estimates. In trajectory simulation, sliding-window ROVO achieved a mean orientation error just 10.7% as large as that of the conventional SLAM baseline. On real flight data, ROVO achieved rotation accuracy comparable to ORB-SLAM3 and DPVO under the original Bell412 settings. With a narrower FoV or at higher flight altitude, ROVO reduced relative rotation RMSE by 19.7--69.4% compared with the next-best method in each comparison. Code and simulation tools are available at https://github.com/sssxxxkkkk/ROVO.
item.dc:creator: Xiaokai Song, Li Zhang, Xichao Teng, Erting Pan, Yibin Ye, Kun Wang, Leqi Liu, Guangcheng Dai

item.title: Even Quartets and the Maximum Density of a Simplical 3-Cocycle
item.description: arXiv:2611.32833v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Colour the triples of an $n$-element set red or blue, and call a four-set even if it contains an even number of red triples. We prove that the minimum number of even four-sets is $\frac5{16}\binom n4-\Theta(n^3)$. In particular, the maximum asymptotic density of a simplicial $3$-cocycle over the field of two elements is $11/16$. The classical two-part matrix construction attains the limiting bound. We prove that it also determines the unique limiting distribution of quartet parities on every fixed number of vertices. Writing $m_n$ for the minimum density, we bound the limit inferior and limit superior of $n(5/16-m_n)$ between $0.75$ and $0.752427$. The lower bound on even quartets follows from an exact rational inequality on eight vertices. A perturbation of the construction explains all $72$ cases of equality in this finite inequality, of which only $22$ survive in an extremal limit.
item.dc:creator: John Mackey

item.title: Moving Geometric Objects to Render Their Intersection Graph Connected or Locally Dense
item.description: arXiv:2609.22958v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study graph editing problems on geometric intersection graphs. For a tuple $\mathcal S=(S_1,\dots,S_n)$ of geometric objects in some Euclidean space, let $G_{\mathcal S}$ be their intersection graph. We study the problem of finding a tuple $D=(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ of movement vectors such that the resulting intersection graph $G_{\mathcal{S}+D}$ (after moving, for every $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$, object $S_i$ by $d_i$) has a predefined property and the total moving distance $\|D\|$ is minimum. In the weighted version, we are also given a weight vector $w=(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ with positive entries, and the objective is to minimise the total weighted moving distance $\|w \cdot D\|$. We first consider the property locally dense, which we define as containment of a $k$-clique. Given $n$ weighted intervals, we solve the problem with respect to this property in $O(k^{1/3} n \log^{1+\varepsilon} n)$ time for any $\varepsilon>0$. We then consider $k$-connectivity for $1\le k \le n-1$. Given $n$ unweighted unit intervals, we solve the problem in $O(n^2 \log n)$ time and, for $k=1$, in $O(n\log n)$ time. For $k=1$, we prove strong NP-hardness on intervals of arbitrary length and on weighted unit disks (with only two distinct weights), and weak NP-hardness on weighted intervals (even when lengths equal weights).
item.dc:creator: Tesshu Hanaka, Nicol\'as Honorato-Droguett, Hirotaka Ono, Samuel Wolf, Alexander Wolff

item.title: Trajectory Visibility at First Sight
item.description: arXiv:2611.29872v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $P$ be a simple polygon with $n$ vertices, and let two moving entities $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ travel at constant (possibly distinct) speeds $v_q$ and $v_r$ along line-segment trajectories $\tau_q$ and $\tau_r$ inside $P$. We study the first-visibility time $ t^* = \min\bigl\{\,t \ge 0 \mid \overline{q(t)\,r(t)} \subseteq P\,\bigr\}, $ the earliest moment at which the segment joining $q(t)$ and $r(t)$ lies entirely within $P$. Prior work by Eades et al.~\cite{swat2020,eeades-phd} focused on the decision version of this question in a simple polygon. They gave a one-shot decision algorithm running in ${O}(n)$ time. For a stationary entity and a moving one, they gave a data structure with ${O}(n \log n)$ preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that answers decision queries in ${O}(\log n)$ time. For two moving entities, after ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ preprocessing time, they built a data structure of size ${O}(n \log^5 n)$ with ${O}(n^{3/4}\log^3 n)$ query time. Variants for polygonal domains with holes or when entities cross the boundary of $P$ lie beyond our scope. In this work, we go beyond decision to compute $t^*$ exactly under three models for a simple polygon $P$. When both trajectories are fixed in advance, we preprocess $P$ in ${O}(n)$ time and space and answer each query $(v_q, v_r)$ in ${O}(\log n)$ time. If one trajectory $\tau_r$ is fixed while $\tau_q$ is given as a query, we build a structure in ${O}(n \log n)$ time and space that computes $t^*$ in ${O}(\log^2 n)$ time per query. When neither trajectory is known in advance, we develop a data structure with ${O}(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ expected preprocessing time and ${O}(n)$ space that achieves ${O}(n^{1/2}\,\text{polylog}(n))$ expected query time for any fixed $\varepsilon > 0$.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Abam, M.A., Ghodsi, M., Kazemi, S.M.H. (2026). Trajectory Visibility at First Sight. In: Di Giacomo, E., Mondal, D. (eds) WALCOM: Algorithms and Computation. WALCOM 2026. Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 16444. Springer, Singapore
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Ali Abam, Mohammad Ghodsi, Seyed Mohammad Hussein Kazemi

item.title: Fast Queries of Fibered Barcodes
item.description: arXiv:2511.05837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The fibered barcode $\mathcal{F}(M)$ of a bipersistence module $M$ is the map sending each non-negatively sloped affine line $\ell \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ to the barcode of the restriction of $M$ along $\ell$. The simplicity, computability, and stability of $\mathcal{F}(M)$ make it a natural choice of invariant for data analysis applications. In an earlier preprint [arXiv:1512.00180], we introduced a framework for real-time interactive visualization of $\mathcal{F}(M)$, which allows the user to select a single line $\ell$ via a GUI and then plots the associated barcode. This visualization is a key feature of our software RIVET for the visualization and analysis of bipersistent homology. Such interactive visualization requires a framework for efficient queries of $\mathcal{F}(M)$, i.e., for quickly obtaining the barcode along a given line $\ell$. To enable such queries, we introduced a novel data structure based on planar line arrangements, called an augmented arrangement. The aim of the present paper is to give an updated and improved exposition of the parts of our preprint [arXiv:1512.00180] concerning the mathematics of the augmented arrangement and its computation. Notably, by taking the input to be a minimal presentation rather than a chain complex, we are able to substantially simplify our main algorithm and its complexity analysis.
item.dc:creator: Michael Lesnick, Matthew Wright

item.title: Polynomial bounds for quasiplanar graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.21416v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A graph $G$ is $k$-quasiplanar if it can be drawn in the plane without $k$ pairwise crossing edges. It was a longstanding conjecture that $n$-vertex $k$-quasiplanar graphs have $O_k(n)$ edges. Recently, using AI tools, we discovered that a theorem in topology proven by Beeker and Lazarovich essentially resolves this conjecture, with the implicit constant depending superexponentially on $k$. In this paper, we greatly improve this bound, showing that every $k$-quasiplanar $n$-vertex graph has at most $O(k^2n)$ edges. Our proof is purely combinatorial, based on a geometric charging scheme and Erd\H{o}s-Szekeres type arguments. We also construct $k$-quasiplanar graphs on $n$ vertices with $\Omega(k^{8/7}n)$, disproving the widely held belief that the right order of magnitude is $\Theta(kn)$.
item.dc:creator: Aleksa Milojevi\'c, Patryk Morawski, J\'anos Pach, Ankan Sadhu, Benny Sudakov, G\'abor Tardos, Istvan Tomon, Ji Zeng
